title: Why a near-round trip in gilts concealed a large real term-premium shock
summary: The small net change in long gilt yields over 2025 conceals a marked change in who was willing to take duration risk and at what price. Lisa Panigrahi and Amarjot Sidhu attribute most of the rise into early September to higher real term premia. Global uncertainty and the volume of bonds coming to market raised the compensation investors required for holding long maturities. In the UK a retreat in demand from traditional buyers and uncertainty about government financing amplified that pressure. In the final quarter, news about the maturity mix of future gilt supply helped reverse it. The analysis is by Bank staff. It neither signals a change in the MPC's preferred path for Bank Rate nor gives a target for long yields.

The sequence matters for assessing performance. From the start of January to the early-September peak, the 30-year yield rose about 50 basis points to 5.7%, against about 20 basis points to 4.8% at ten years. By year-end the 30-year was near 5.2%, around four basis points above its starting point, while the ten-year was near 4.5%, around twelve basis points lower. The UK therefore experienced both an intra-year steepening and a substantial subsequent flattening, while retaining some net steepening across the year. Chart 1 compares spot-yield changes over two horizons. Chart 2 plots the cumulative change in the 30-year less 10-year spread. The US and German curves shared the initial steepening but retained much more of it. Chart 3 compares levels in per cent across seven countries. The UK's position near the upper edge is partly attributable to relatively high short rates and does not by itself identify a peculiarly British risk premium. These charts use data to 19 December.

The authors use a different instrument to identify what happened further out. A spot gilt yield incorporates rates from today to maturity. A five-year rate starting five years ahead reduces the influence of near-term policy decisions. Figure A separates a nominal yield along two dimensions, expected short rates versus risk compensation and real versus inflation components. In Chart 4 the real term-premium contribution to the cumulative change in the forward yield is positive through much of the year, then smaller in the final quarter. Declining inflation risk compensation offsets part of that rise. Expected inflation and expected real policy rates contribute relatively little over the year, although lower expected short rates also contributed to the late decline in long yields. The component bars are model estimates using data to 18 December. The survey evidence on anchored medium-term inflation expectations provides a separate check on that interpretation. Neither directly measures what compensation an individual gilt buyer demanded.

The distinction between the international and domestic explanations rests on different evidence. Common moves and conversations with market participants support a global premium associated with geopolitical and trade uncertainty, elevated sovereign issuance and concern about fiscal sustainability. Domestically, increases in yields had improved the funding position of defined-benefit pension schemes and reduced some of their need to buy long gilts. Buyers comparing gilts with foreign bonds and other assets faced less compulsion to own that maturity. The authors infer that a given global shock could consequently produce a larger UK response. They offer no quantitative split between those channels. Earlier in the year investors also cited uncertainty about the government's fiscal headroom and future borrowing.

The change in the supply outlook illustrates the importance of distinguishing total borrowing from the maturity of debt offered. The Debt Management Office cancelled a long auction in early September and announced a smaller long-maturity share of issuance at the November Budget. Fiscal expectations had also shifted before the Budget, and the outcome broadly met them. Market contacts viewed these developments as important to the fall in yields. Separately, the MPC approved a £70 billion reduction in the stock of gilts held for monetary policy over October 2025 to September 2026. The Bank intended relatively fewer sales in the long sector. The stock reduction is not a measure of long bonds sold. The authors cite highly uncertain staff estimates of only a modest effect of quantitative tightening on term premia since the programme began in February 2022.

For the MPC, higher long rates can lower asset valuations and raise borrowing costs for large companies. The authors expect a smaller effect on output and inflation than from an equal increase in shorter rates, especially two- to five-year swap rates that influence household borrowing. The financial stability issue differs. Gilts provide collateral, so a sharp adjustment can spread into repo funding before the macroeconomic effects of higher discount rates appear. Stronger LDI resilience since 2022 qualifies that comparison. The note gives reasons to monitor the speed and financing of a sell-off alongside its size, without estimating a threshold at which instability would begin.

questions.question: How robust is the attribution to real term premia across models and instruments?
questions.detail: Chart 4 shows a sizeable positive real-premium contribution offset partly by declining inflation risk compensation. This matters because a hedge against expected MPC tightening could perform quite differently from an exposure to long real duration. Compare the cited term-structure specifications, gilt forwards, inflation-linked pricing and contemporaneous survey expectations using a common data cut. Examine whether the dominant component survives plausible changes in the decomposition.

questions.question: How much duration did investors actually expect to absorb after each supply announcement?
questions.detail: Market contacts link the September and November announcements to the UK reversal. The article does not quantify the change relative to prior issuance expectations or isolate simultaneous fiscal news. Reconstruct the maturity-weighted change from the DMO remit, auctions and Bank sale schedules, and compare gilts and swaps around the releases against comparable foreign maturities. The result would help distinguish a repeatable supply sensitivity from a one-off surprise.

questions.question: When would an orderly repricing of duration become a funding problem?
questions.detail: The article identifies collateral and repo channels while noting stronger LDI resilience. It does not quantify how much variation margin or refinancing need a particular move would generate. Examine the cited Financial Stability Reports and system-wide exploratory scenario evidence on liquid buffers, collateral calls and repo availability. Those constraints matter for how reliably a long-gilt hedge could be financed through a volatile interval.
